endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: The data powering the AI system must reflect current knowledge, necessitating continuous checks to determine the frequency of data updates for open clinical trials, treatment indications, guidelines, and biomarker-selection criteria.

evidence.title: EviLedger: governing clinical AI with a verifiable evidence ledger
evidence.outcome: Detection and triage of actionable guideline changes versus manual surveillance
evidence.effect: 6-month hospital pilot: 5.5× more actionable guideline changes detected with 104× faster triage than manual surveillance
evidence.quote: In a 6-month hospital pilot, EviLedger detects 5.5× more actionable guideline changes with 104× faster triage than manual surveillance.

evidence.title: Large-scale observational study of AI-based patient and surgical material verification system in ophthalmology: real-world evaluation in 37 529 cases
evidence.outcome: Errors from IOL models not in AI training due to delayed updates
evidence.effect: 7.3% of 9713 post-implementation IOL surgeries involved unlearned lenses, leading to two incorrect IOL implantations; model updated only three times due to budget and stability constraints.
evidence.quote: Of the 9713 IOL surgeries performed post implementation, 7.3% involved unlearned lenses, leading to two cases of incorrect IOL implantation.

evidence.title: The exciting potential for ChatGPT in obstetrics and gynecology
evidence.venue: American journal of obstetrics and gynecology
evidence.outcome: Currency of ChatGPT's training data and clinical knowledge in obstetrics and gynecology answers
evidence.effect: Training data were not readily updated; the model did not reliably (if at all) source data from after 2021, so answers can be outdated.
evidence.quote: The specific model that was assessed here, seems to not reliably (if at all) source data from after 2021.

evidence.title: Annual updates of the European Association of Urology - European Society for Pediatric Urology (EAU-ESPU) paediatric urology guidelines: Are large-language models (LLM) better than the usual structured methodology?
evidence.outcome: LLM ability to incorporate recent literature into guideline updates
evidence.effect: All three LLMs were unable to update the guidelines with recent relevant literature due to lack of access to correct scientific databases.
evidence.quote: All three LLMs were unable to update the guidelines with the recent relevant literature because of the lack of access to the correct scientific databases.

commentary.bottom_line: One preprint hospital pilot suggests that automated surveillance may detect 5.5 times more actionable guideline changes and triage them 104 times faster than manual review, but no study has tested whether a set update frequency keeps AI outputs current or reduces patient harm. Three hazard studies show that AI systems fall out of date, with one deployment linking delayed updates to two incorrect lens implantations.

perspectives.view: A single level 5 preprint (n=3200 guideline-change events) tests part of the practice. It measures detection and triage speed, not the currency of AI outputs or patient outcomes, so the evidence is indirect. It has no replication and no peer review. Certainty starts low and drops to very low for indirectness and imprecision.

In a Japanese deployment, 7.3% of 9713 post-implementation surgeries involved lenses the model had not learned, and two patients received incorrect implants. The model was updated only three times. This shows the harm that stale knowledge can cause. It does not show that a fixed update schedule would have prevented those errors.

The pilot ran in a real hospital for six months and reports faster triage than manual surveillance, which suggests automated change detection may be workable in practice. Two offline studies found that language models used knowledge from before 2021 and could not reach current literature databases. Those findings suggest that update cycles depend on data access as well as scheduling.

The lens model was updated only three times because of budget and stability constraints. This suggests that update frequency competes with cost and validation workload. The pilot's reported 104-fold faster triage may lower the staff time needed for surveillance, but the study does not report costs.

The CHAI Assurance Standards Guide states that data powering AI systems must reflect current knowledge. It calls for continuous checks to set update frequency for trials, indications, guidelines, and biomarker criteria. This is a voluntary framework rather than a binding rule, and no study in this set examines regulatory requirements for update schedules.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares AI systems with and without a defined update frequency on output accuracy, time to incorporate guideline changes, or patient harm. Peer-reviewed replication of automated guideline surveillance, with cost reporting and links to downstream AI behavior, is also missing.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and the one pilot did not describe its patient population. It remains unknown whether update schedules perform differently in settings with fewer informatics staff or smaller budgets, where the lens study suggests update cycles may lag.
